heading: Islands of the Malabar trade
body: Lakshadweep — around three dozen small coral islands scattered across the Arabian Sea off India's southwestern coast — has never had a history separate from the Malabar coast of Kerala facing it. Most of its inhabitants descend from settlers who arrived from that coast before the 7th century CE, and the islands appear in outside sources as early as the 1st century CE, when a Greek sailor's account mentions them as a source of tortoiseshell. For most of their history the islands were governed as an extension of mainland Malabar power rather than as an independent territory: before 1100 CE a small Hindu kingdom on the coast annexed them, and after the fall of Kerala's Kulashekhara dynasty in 1102 they passed to the Kolathiri rajas of northern Malabar.

Islam reached the islands early and thoroughly. Arab traders were sailing this stretch of the Indian Ocean route for centuries, and continued contact together with missionary activity from the 7th century onward led to the conversion of the entire island population to Islam — traditional island accounts credit the Arab missionary Ubaidullah, though as with much oral tradition the precise date is not independently verifiable. Tradition also holds that control passed, after a Kolathiri princess married a Muslim convert, to a separate Muslim-ruled dynasty based at Cannanore, the Arakkal family — though the Lakshadweep administration's own official history instead dates the Arakkal family's takeover of administrative control to around the middle of the 16th century, a few centuries later than the marriage story implies; the two accounts may describe a religious/dynastic tradition and a later, separately documented administrative transfer rather than the same event, but this page does not reconcile them. Sovereignty is recorded as remaining with the Hindu Kolathiri (Chirakkal) raja even after the islands' conversion to Islam.

Administratively, Lakshadweep only became a distinct unit of Indian government in living memory. During the linguistic reorganisation of Indian states in 1956, the islands were separated from Madras State's Malabar district and constituted as their own union territory, then called the Laccadive, Minicoy and Amindivi Islands; it took its current name, Lakshadweep, in 1973.

The result is a territory whose history is inseparable from Kerala's — the same pepper-and-spice trade routes, the same seafaring Arab and Malabar merchant communities — but expressed on a scatter of coral islands whose isolation preserved a distinctly Islamic maritime culture found nowhere else on the Indian coast.
